units.name: The River Nile and its floodplain
Nile risks and the GERD rivalry

leitner_plan.new: The Nile, floodplains and the GERD (6)

cards.title: Water as a natural resource
cards.question: What is a natural resource, and why is water so important?
points: A natural resource is something produced naturally on Earth's surface, such as water, gold or wood.
Water is vital for the health of the planet, animals and people.
Water is stored in the atmosphere, in rivers, in the soil and in the ocean.
The water cycle describes how water moves between the ocean, the atmosphere and the land.
About 70% of all freshwater used in the world is used for agriculture (farming).
cards.watch_out: The water cycle is a process of movement, not just a list of places where water is stored.
cards.hook: Store and move: stores are places, the cycle is movement.
cards.grade9: Link water to development: in an LIC (income below $1,100 per person per year) a lack of clean water can hold back health and work.

cards.title: River features
cards.question: What are the main features of a river?
points: A river is a natural moving body of water that transports water over the land towards the sea.
Source: the beginning of the river, on high ground. Mouth: the end, where it meets the sea, on low lying land.
River channel: the landform the river flows through. Tributary: a small river that joins a larger river.
Valley: a low area between hills formed by a river. Floodplain: flat, fertile land on either side of a river.
Water gets into rivers from precipitation, over the land and through the soil.
cards.watch_out: The source is on high ground and the mouth is on low ground. Rivers always flow downhill.
cards.hook: Source at the top, mouth at the bottom, like a person drinking.
cards.grade9: Explain why floodplains are flat: sediment is spread evenly across them during floods.

cards.title: Drainage and deltas
cards.question: What happens when a river reaches the sea?
points: Near the sea the land is flat, so the river slows down and deposits (drops) the sediment it carries.
Sediment builds up and can force the river to split into smaller channels called distributaries.
This forms a delta, such as the Nile Delta in northern Egypt.
Deltas have very fertile soil, so they are good for farming.
cards.watch_out: Tributaries join a river; distributaries split away from it near the mouth.
cards.grade9: Use a satellite image of the Nile Delta to describe its triangle shape and dense farmland.

cards.title: The River Nile
cards.question: Where is the River Nile, and where does it begin and end?
points: The Nile is a major river in north-east Africa. At about 6,650 km it is the longest river in the world.
Its sources are Lake Victoria (White Nile) and the Ethiopian Highlands (Blue Nile).
The White and Blue Nile join in Sudan.
It flows from south to north and its mouth is the Mediterranean Sea.
The floodplains of the Nile are densely populated. Cairo, with over 22 million people, is built on the floodplain.
cards.watch_out: The Nile flows north, so on a map it flows up the page. Many students think rivers always flow down the page.
cards.hook: White from Victoria, Blue from Ethiopia, meet in Sudan.
cards.grade9: Explain why people live on the floodplain even though Egypt is a desert: it is the only fertile, watered land.

cards.title: How the Nile floodplain formed
cards.question: How did the floodplain of the River Nile form?
points: Before: heavy rainfall in the Ethiopian Highlands each summer adds lots of water to the Blue Nile.
The river transports sediment (soil and silt) from the highlands downstream.
During: the river overflows its banks and floods the flat land beside the channel.
As the water spreads out it slows down and deposits the sediment, which is nutrient rich.
After: the water drains away and the sediment is left behind. Over many floods it builds up into flat, fertile land.

example.heading: Key words to use
lines: heavy rainfall, transport, sediment, overflows, river bank, deposits, build up, flat, fertile, nutrient rich, crops, wheat

cards.watch_out: This is the key lesson for the written test. Explain before, during and after the flood in order.
cards.hook: Rain, carry, spill, drop, build: the floodplain story.
cards.grade9: Link formation to people: the fertile sediment lets farmers grow crops like wheat, so populations have thrived in Egypt for over 6,000 years.

cards.title: Uses and features of floodplains
cards.question: What are floodplains like and how are they used?
points: Floodplains are flat land with nutrient rich soils.
They form when rivers deposit sediment during floods.
They are used for agriculture (crops such as wheat and oranges along the Nile) and for building towns and cities.
Egypt is very arid (about 20 mm of rain a year), so the Nile floodplain is where most Egyptians live.
cards.watch_out: Floodplains are useful but risky: building on them can put homes in danger when the river floods.
cards.grade9: Weigh up benefits and risks of living on a floodplain to show balanced thinking.

cards.title: Uses of the Nile and overextraction
cards.question: How is the Nile used, and why is overextraction a risk?
points: The Nile is used for agriculture (most of all), in industry and in homes.
Overextraction means removing too much of a natural resource.
Demand for water is rising because of population growth and rising wealth.
Overextraction happens when water demand is greater than water supply. About 82 billion cubic metres are taken from the Nile each year.
cards.watch_out: Agriculture uses by far the most Nile water in Egypt, not homes.
cards.grade9: Explain why rising wealth increases demand: richer people use more water at home and buy more food and goods.

cards.title: The GERD
cards.question: What is the GERD and why did Ethiopia build it?
points: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) is a huge dam on the Blue Nile in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia is an LIC with a fast growing economy.
Reasons for building it: to generate hydroelectric power and to secure a water supply.
Ethiopia uses the electricity to power industry and to sell to other countries. Only about half of Ethiopians have access to electricity.
cards.watch_out: The GERD is on the Blue Nile in Ethiopia, not in Egypt or Sudan.
cards.grade9: Explain Ethiopia's view: about 80% of the Nile's water comes from Ethiopia, so it feels it should be able to use it.

cards.title: River rivals: impacts of the GERD
cards.question: What are the positive and negative impacts of the GERD, and why are Egypt and Ethiopia rivals?
points: Positive: hydroelectric power and an improved water supply for Ethiopia.
Negative: increased political tensions in the region and reduced water supply for Egypt and Sudan.
Egypt says a 1959 agreement gives it most (66%) of the Nile's water and the power to stop projects on the river.
Ethiopia says this is unfair because most of the water comes from its land.
cards.watch_out: Always give both perspectives (Egypt and Ethiopia) when you explain the rivalry.
cards.hook: Power for Ethiopia, worry for Egypt.
cards.grade9: Reach a judgement: was building the GERD a good idea? Weigh development for Ethiopia against risks for Egypt.

cards.title: Food security
cards.question: What are food security and food insecurity?
points: Food security is having access to enough nutritious food. Food insecurity is lacking it.
Countries ensure food security by growing food or importing it.
About 3 billion people are food insecure, and the number is rising.
Food insecurity causes malnutrition. This leads to stunted growth in children and more disease, reducing people's ability to work.
cards.watch_out: Food insecurity is not the same as famine. Famine is an extreme, widespread lack of food; food insecurity can be less severe.
cards.grade9: Link causes: conflict is a major cause, as 70% of food insecure people live in places affected by conflict, such as Yemen and Syria.

cards.title: Patterns of food consumption
cards.question: How is food consumption measured, and what is the global pattern?
points: Food consumption is how much energy is gained from food, measured in calories.
The global trend is rising: from about 2,180 calories per person per day in 1961 to about 2,950 in 2020.
The pattern is uneven: highest in HICs (often over 3,200 calories), lowest in some LICs (under 2,000), especially parts of Africa.
Richer countries usually consume more calories.
cards.watch_out: Describe a pattern with continents and examples, not just the word uneven.
cards.grade9: Use data in your answer: quote numbers and name countries from the map.

cards.title: Latitude and global rainfall
cards.question: What is latitude, and what is the global pattern of rainfall?
points: Latitude is the distance of a place north or south of the equator, measured in degrees.
Low latitudes are near the equator; high latitudes are near the poles.
Rainfall occurs in horizontal bands around the planet, a bit like a zebra crossing.
Drought is a long period of low rainfall. Low rainfall makes it hard to farm crops, reducing food supply.
cards.watch_out: Lines of latitude run across (horizontally), but they measure distance north or south.
cards.hook: Latitude is flat-itude: lines run flat across the map.
cards.grade9: Name the key lines: equator 0°, Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn 23°, Arctic and Antarctic Circles 66°.

cards.title: Air pressure and rainfall
cards.question: How does air pressure affect rainfall?
points: Air pressure is the force of the atmosphere on the Earth's surface.
Air pressure is also found in horizontal bands around the planet.
Low pressure: air is heated, rises, cools and condenses into clouds, giving precipitation (high rainfall), such as at the equator.
High pressure: air sinks, so clouds do not form and there is low rainfall, such as around 30° north and south (deserts like Egypt).
cards.watch_out: Low pressure means high rainfall, and high pressure means low rainfall. They are opposites.
cards.hook: Low pressure, lots of rain. High pressure, hardly any.
cards.grade9: Explain why Brazil (rainforest, about 230 cm of rain a year) and Egypt (desert) are so different using pressure bands.

cards.title: Soils and food security
cards.question: What makes soil fertile, and where are fertile and infertile soils found?
points: Soil is structured in horizontal layers: topsoil, subsoil, rock pieces, bedrock. A soil profile is a diagram that shows these layers.
The topsoil is the uppermost layer and contains the most nutrients.
Fertile soils need thick topsoil, water and a good structure. Nutrients come from decomposing leaves (the nutrient cycle).
Fertile soils are found in temperate rainy regions, such as the UK and Ireland. Infertile soils are found in hot arid regions, such as Egypt and Syria.
cards.watch_out: Hot arid soils have a thin topsoil with few nutrients and sandy subsoil, which is why farming is hard there.
cards.hook: Nutrient cycle: decompose, release, take up.
cards.grade9: Link soil to food security: countries with fertile soils and no conflict, such as Finland and Ireland, rank highest for food security.

cards.title: Core facts checklist
cards.question: Can you answer each short prompt from the core knowledge list?
points: Source of the Nile: Lake Victoria (White Nile) and the Ethiopian Highlands (Blue Nile). Mouth: Mediterranean Sea. Flow: south to north.
Floodplain: flat, fertile land formed by deposition during floods. Used for farming and building.
Overextraction: water demand exceeding supply. GERD: dam on the Blue Nile for hydroelectric power and water security.
Food security: access to enough nutritious food. About 3 billion people are food insecure.
Low pressure = high rainfall. Fertile soils in temperate rainy regions; infertile in hot arid regions.
cards.watch_out: The test uses the exact short prompts from the core knowledge list. Learn each response word for word.

written.q: Explain how the floodplain of the River Nile formed. Use before, during and after the flood.
model: Before: heavy rainfall in the Ethiopian Highlands adds water to the Blue Nile (1)
The river transports sediment downstream (1)
During: the river overflows its banks onto the flat land (1)
The water slows down and deposits nutrient rich sediment (1)
After: the water drains away, leaving the sediment behind (1)
Over many floods the sediment builds up into flat, fertile land used for crops such as wheat (1)

written.q: Explain why Egypt and Ethiopia are river rivals.
model: Ethiopia built the GERD on the Blue Nile (1)
For hydroelectric power and to secure its water supply (1)
Egypt fears a reduced water supply for farming and homes (1)
Egypt is very arid and depends on the Nile (1)
Egypt says a 1959 agreement gives it most of the Nile's water (1)
Ethiopia says this is unfair because about 80% of the water comes from Ethiopia (1)

written.q: Explain how air pressure affects rainfall.
model: At low pressure, warm air rises (1)
The air cools and water vapour condenses into clouds, giving rain (1)
At high pressure, air sinks (1)
So clouds do not form and there is little rain, as in deserts (1)

written.q: Explain the impacts of food insecurity on people and society.
model: Food insecurity causes malnutrition (1)
Malnutrition causes stunted growth in children (1)
It increases the risk of disease (1)
This reduces people's ability to work, affecting the economy (1)

exam_tips.timing: Chromebook test: 30 questions in the lesson. Written piece: plan for 5 minutes, then write in full sentences.
section_a: Learn every short prompt and response on the core knowledge list.
Watch out for opposites, such as source and mouth, high and low pressure.
Read all four options before choosing.
section_b: For the floodplain question, use the key words and go in order before, during, after.
Give both perspectives (Egypt and Ethiopia) when you write about the GERD.
Use numbers and named places as evidence.

mcq.q: What is a natural resource?
mcq.a: Something produced naturally on Earth's surface, such as water
mcq.e: Examples are water, gold and wood.

mcq.q: Where is water stored?
mcq.a: In the atmosphere, rivers, soil and ocean
mcq.e: These are the water stores.

mcq.q: What is the water cycle?
mcq.a: How water moves between ocean, atmosphere and land
w: A store of water in a lake
mcq.e: It is a process of movement.

mcq.q: What is the income of a low income country (LIC)?
mcq.a: Below $1,100 per person per year
mcq.e: LICs have low income per person.

mcq.q: What is the source of a river?
mcq.a: The beginning of the river, on high ground
w: A small river that joins a larger one
mcq.e: Rivers start on high ground.

mcq.q: What is the mouth of a river?
mcq.a: Where the river meets the sea, on low lying land
mcq.e: It is the end of the river.

mcq.q: What is a tributary?
mcq.a: A small river that joins a larger river
mcq.e: Tributaries add water to the main river.

mcq.q: What is a floodplain?
mcq.a: Flat fertile land on either side of a river
w: High ground where a river starts
mcq.e: It forms from deposited sediment.

mcq.q: What is a valley?
mcq.a: A low area of land between hills formed by a river
mcq.e: Rivers carve valleys over time.

mcq.q: What percentage of global freshwater is used for agriculture?
mcq.a: About 70%
mcq.e: Farming uses the most water.

mcq.q: Where is the River Nile?
mcq.a: North-east Africa
mcq.e: It flows through Egypt.

mcq.q: Where is the source of the White Nile?
mcq.a: Lake Victoria
mcq.e: The Blue Nile starts in the Ethiopian Highlands.

mcq.q: Where is the source of the Blue Nile?
mcq.a: The Ethiopian Highlands
mcq.e: Heavy summer rain falls there.

mcq.q: Where is the mouth of the River Nile?
mcq.a: The Mediterranean Sea
mcq.e: It ends in the Nile Delta.

mcq.q: In which direction does the Nile flow?
mcq.a: South to north
mcq.e: It flows from the highlands to the Mediterranean.

mcq.q: In which country do the White and Blue Nile join?
mcq.a: Sudan
mcq.e: They meet near Khartoum in Sudan.

mcq.q: Why are the floodplains of the Nile densely populated?
mcq.a: The land is flat and fertile with water nearby
w: There is lots of rain there
mcq.e: The rest of Egypt is desert.

mcq.q: How does a floodplain form?
mcq.a: Rivers deposit sediment during times of flood
mcq.e: Sediment builds up over many floods.

mcq.q: Why does the Blue Nile flood each summer?
mcq.a: Heavy rainfall in the Ethiopian Highlands
mcq.e: The rain fills the river.

mcq.q: What makes floodplain soil fertile?
mcq.a: Nutrient rich sediment deposited by floods
mcq.e: Silt carries nutrients.

mcq.q: Which is a use of a floodplain?
mcq.a: Agriculture
mcq.e: Floodplains are used for farming and building.

mcq.q: Roughly how long is the River Nile?
mcq.e: It is the longest river in the world.

mcq.q: What is overextraction?
mcq.a: Removing too much of a natural resource
mcq.e: It happens when demand exceeds supply.

mcq.q: What is the Nile mostly used for?
mcq.a: Agriculture
mcq.e: Irrigation of crops like wheat uses the most water.

mcq.q: Why is demand for water increasing?
mcq.a: Rising population and rising wealth
mcq.e: More people and richer people use more water.

mcq.q: What is the GERD?
mcq.a: A huge dam built along the Blue Nile in Ethiopia
mcq.e: Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.

mcq.q: Why did Ethiopia build the GERD?
mcq.a: To generate hydroelectric power and secure water supply
w: To stop the Nile flooding Egypt
To make a border with Sudan
mcq.e: It supports Ethiopia's development.

mcq.q: How does Ethiopia use the hydroelectric power from the GERD?
mcq.a: To power industry and to sell to other countries
w: To pump water to Egypt for free
mcq.e: Many neighbours want to buy the electricity.

mcq.q: Which is a negative impact of the GERD?
mcq.a: Reduced water supply for Egypt and Sudan
mcq.e: Egypt fears it will not have enough water.

mcq.q: Which is a positive impact of the GERD?
mcq.a: Hydroelectric power for Ethiopia
mcq.e: It brings energy to an LIC.

mcq.q: How would you describe Ethiopia's economy?
mcq.a: An LIC with a fast growing economy
mcq.e: It is developing quickly.

mcq.q: What is food security?
mcq.a: Having access to enough nutritious food
mcq.e: Food insecurity is the opposite.

mcq.q: About how many people are food insecure?
mcq.a: 3 billion
mcq.e: And the number is rising.

mcq.q: What does food insecurity cause?
mcq.a: Malnutrition
mcq.e: Lack of nutritious food causes malnutrition.

mcq.q: What is an impact of malnutrition on society?
mcq.a: Stunted growth and more disease, reducing ability to work
mcq.e: Health problems affect the economy too.

mcq.q: How is food consumption measured?
mcq.a: In calories
mcq.e: Calories measure the energy from food.

mcq.q: What is the trend of global food consumption?
mcq.a: It is rising
w: It goes up and down every year
mcq.e: From about 2,180 to 2,950 calories per day.

mcq.q: How would you describe the global pattern of food consumption?
mcq.a: Uneven
mcq.e: HICs usually consume more.

mcq.q: How can a country ensure food security?
mcq.a: By growing food or importing it
mcq.e: Both methods increase supply.

mcq.q: What is latitude?
mcq.a: The distance north or south of the equator in degrees
w: The distance east or west of London
mcq.e: Low latitudes are near the equator.

mcq.q: Where are high latitudes?
mcq.a: Near the poles
mcq.e: High latitudes are 60 to 90 degrees.

mcq.q: What is air pressure?
mcq.a: The force of the atmosphere on Earth's surface
mcq.e: It is found in horizontal bands.

mcq.q: Which type of pressure brings high rainfall?
mcq.a: Low pressure
mcq.e: Rising air cools and condenses into clouds.

mcq.q: What is a drought?
mcq.a: A long period of low rainfall
mcq.e: Droughts reduce food supply.

mcq.q: Where are fertile soils found?
mcq.a: In temperate rainy regions
mcq.e: The UK and Ireland have fertile soils.

mcq.q: Which layer of soil contains the most nutrients?
mcq.a: Topsoil
mcq.e: It is the uppermost layer.

mcq.q: What three things make soil fertile?
mcq.a: Thick topsoil, water and good structure
mcq.e: Decomposing leaves add nutrients.

mcq.q: What does a soil profile show?
mcq.a: The layers of soil
w: Where soils are on a map
mcq.e: It is a cross section diagram.

vocab.meaning: Small pieces of soil, sand and rock carried by water
vocab.example: The Nile carries sediment from the Ethiopian Highlands.

vocab.meaning: To drop or leave material behind
vocab.example: When the river slows down it will deposit sediment.

vocab.meaning: Rich in nutrients and good for growing crops
vocab.example: The floodplain is fertile because of the sediment.

vocab.meaning: A small river that joins a larger river
vocab.example: A tributary adds more water to the main river.

vocab.meaning: A person or group competing with another
vocab.example: Egypt sees Ethiopia as a rival over the Nile.

vocab.meaning: Poor health caused by not having enough nutritious food
vocab.example: Malnutrition can cause stunted growth in children.

vocab.meaning: A long period of low rainfall
vocab.example: A drought makes it hard to grow crops.

vocab.meaning: A chemical that plants and animals need to grow and stay healthy
vocab.example: Decomposing leaves add each nutrient back into the soil.
